newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria puts brave face on NATO summit decision.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria puts brave face on NATO summit decision.

text.p: Bulgaria on Wednesday put a brave face on the results of NATO's enlargement summit but newspapers said the fact Sofia was not mentioned as a potential member meant it probably would not make a second round of expansion either.

"The most important thing for Bulgaria is that the process of enlargement has been launched in Madrid and the NATO gates have been opened for new member states," foreign ministry spokesman Radko Vlaikov told a news conference.

"If reforms in the country proceed at the same pace as they have in the past several months, when the alliance comes to decide on the second group of countries to be invited to join, we will be ready."

Newspapers were less diplomatic in their assessment of NATO's decision to invite only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic into the Western security bloc and mention only Romania and Slovenia as deserving cases for membership.
"NATO is forgetting us," said a headline in Kontinent daily. "Only Greece and Turkey back us in Madrid." Standart's headline read, "NATO cuts us off for second wave".

Bulgaria, which made a clear statement of its desire to join NATO only in February, was realistic about its dim chances of joining immediately but had hoped for reassurance that it would be considered next time round.
"The point now is to admit that we have nobody but ourselves to blame," Kontinent daily said in an editorial.

"Bulgaria's policy towards NATO has been more than odd during the last seven years. We even went so far as to say at the time of (former Socialist prime minister) Zhan Videnov 'we want to join you but you must ask Russia'."
The Socialist government, ousted from power by street protests in January and February, had been ambivalent on NATO membership for fear of upsetting its traditional allies in Moscow.
"Bulgaria will not make it to NATO even in the second wave. Our neighbours gave us support, the U.S. invited us to lunch, but only three new members are welcome," said the Socialist daily Douma.
Bulgaria has slashed government spending as part of IMF-prescribed reforms but lacks the cash to modernise its armed forces to NATO standards.
Armed Forces Chief of Staff General Miho Mihov said on Monday he wanted to modernise the army and improve its rapid reaction capability but officers were struggling even to keep conscripts fed.
"The problem is dramatic," he said. "We will have to cut expenses before the end of the year because more than half the budget has been spent already."
